data.title: Schumer: 'Trump just gave Putin the best birthday gift he'll get this year'
data.description:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) accused President Trump on Saturday of giving Russian President Vladimir Putin “the best birthday gift” after he waived new sanctions on Russia days before they were set to take effect.

“By giving the Russian economy life support Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier,” Schumer wrote in a post on the social platform X. “There’s nothing America First about Trump caving in to Putin and exempting Russia from US sanctions.”

A sweeping legislative package Trump signed into law last month would have imposed tariffs up to 100 percent on the top five purchasers of Russian fuel. The president’s Friday night executive order puts those sanctions on hold. 

The move follows Trump’s decision last week to lift sanctions on Russian diesel products, allowing the country to “immediately” export 300,000 tons to the U.S. and the greater world economy amid global fuel shortages. The deal drew swift bipartisan pushback. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said these relief actions will further endanger his citizens, as Ukraine continues to fight back in a yearslong war against Russia. 

On Saturday, the Ukrainian leader warned the “sanctions relief will continue” in a social media post. 

Zelensky mourned the loss of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who the Russian sanctions package was named after and who pushed for more U.S. support to Ukraine during the war effort. 

“It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest,” Zelensky wrote. “I want to thank both Democrats and Republicans who supported his bill. That was a major victory: this truly bipartisan support. 

“And now, the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” he continued. “And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people. This certainly does not stop the war.”

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), the top Democrat on Congress’s Joint Economic Committee, expressed his disapproval with the president’s new executive order in a statement released by his office late Friday evening. 

“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said.

“Trump has proven he will twist this law and abuse the powers it conferred on him, and while he has let the tariff powers lie for the moment, the law as written also empowers Trump to weaponize new trade authorities against our allies and trading partners,” the Democrat continued. “Congress must fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure it truly supports Ukraine.” 

Several Republican lawmakers also joined in on criticizing this relief, with retiring Texas Sen. John Cornyn posting on social media that “Lindsey would be appalled,” in reference to his late Republican colleague from South Carolina. 

Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a frequent critic of the Trump administration, called the relief “beyond irresponsible” in a statement shared on social media.

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis said. “If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”

data.title: Rahm Emanuel tries out a new primary lane: Democratic 'consultant in chief'
data.description:
Rahm Emanuel isn’t waiting for the 2028 presidential race to officially begin. 

The former congressman turned White House chief of staff, Chicago mayor and U.S. ambassador to Japan has been making the rounds in South Carolina, the first state on the Democratic presidential primary calendar.

For the second time in recent months, he spent a couple of days this past week, appearing at fundraisers and campaigning for midterm candidates, while pushing his own strategy and message. 

Emanuel has been to other early states too, including Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan, campaigning alongside candidates running in the midterms but also making clear his intentions and political ambitions. 

He has also become a near-permanent fixture on the airwaves, outperforming all of his potential competitors in the presidential race. 

In the last few weeks, Emanuel has been everywhere, appearing on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” a NewsNation town hall with Chris Cuomo, PBS’s “Overheard With Evan Smith,” and Fox News host Sean Hannity’s podcast, which went on for two hours. 

“He loves the hustle, and he loves the game, and no one is likely to take more meetings or make more phone calls a day,” Democratic strategist Eddie Vale said. 

Emanuel isn’t simply testing the waters, political observers say. He has sought to drive the conversation with ideas, playing what one donor called “the Democratic consultant-in-chief,” trying to fill a void at a time when Democrats have been thirsty for leadership.

But in many ways, his views run counter to the energy in the left flank of the party, where democratic socialist candidates have been gaining steam. 

In an interview this week on SiriusXM’s “The Briefing With Steve Scully,” Emanuel said Democrats shouldn’t seek the impeachment of President Trump if they win the House in the midterm elections.

Instead, he said Democrats should pursue an ethics package. 

“In 2026, in three weeks from now, the Republicans are going to lose the election. What the Democrats do in 2027 will determine whether we won the election by bringing change,” Emanuel told Scully. “An ethics package brings change. A raise in the minimum wage 20 bucks by 2030 is bringing change. 

“You do impeachment, it’s just another food fight,” Emanuel added. “I’m offended by everything this president has done. He has literally turned the Oval Office into eBay on steroids. Get change. Deliver that.”

In an interview with The Hill, Scully said Emanuel “wants to make sure his voice is heard” during the precampaign season. 

“I think he would like to be president. I think he is trying to set the debate up for the party,” Scully said. “I think he’s trying to get ahead of the game to plant his flag in the more centrist wing of the party.”

“He wants to lead that battle,” Scully said, adding that Emanuel isn’t just speaking to Democratic audiences but traveling to red states including Mississippi and Louisiana. “I think he’s casting a wide canvas on where he sees the party going.”

By campaigning early, particularly while other would-be candidates are busy governing or campaigning, Scully said, “it gives Rahm a clear path right now.”

Emanuel has also tried to make the case that Democrats can continue to push affordability along with corruption, saying the two issues are “heads and tails of the same coin.”

“The president of the United States gets a $450 million gift from Qatar — Air Force One — and you’re getting $4.50 a gallon of gas,” he added.

John Morgan, an injury lawyer and Democratic mega-donor, said Emanuel is appealing to voters because “he tells it like it is.” 

“I love everything about him,” Morgan added. “His positions are very well thought out and he articulates them succinctly and effectively. 

“He’s very brash and direct. The question is will that sell?”

Other Democrats say Emanuel is the wrong messenger for the party at this moment.

“He is seen as part of the establishment,” one Democratic strategist said. “And that’s going to be his biggest obstacle: How does he bring people along when they largely want to move away from the past?” 

One Democratic donor, who asked for anonymity to express their authentic views, said Emanuel is “really smart, really experienced, but abrasive [and] incredibly disliked.”

Still, the donor added that Emanuel has sought to soften his approach since his days in the White House and in Congress. 

“A lot of people are liking what they hear because he’s taking a [more] pragmatic approach than ever before,” the donor said. “He’s a sharp-elbowed, pit-bull kind of guy, but lately he’s acting in a much softer way.” 

Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist who does not support Trump, said Emanuel “right now is the only Democrat I could support.” 

“What he’s doing is doing a great service for the Democratic Party,” Del Percio said. “He’s trying to take away some of the stigmas from the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] that keeps the party’s approval rating so low. He’s trying to start a primary in such a way that can be appealing to voters. 

“When you look at his tour, if you will, it’s all about setting up an agenda of what Dems are for, and also how they can appeal to the swing states that it will take to win a general election in 2028,” she said. 

Del Percio specifically pointed to Emanuel’s comments about how the DSA wants to be its own party. 

“The Dems are all talking about having this big tent,” she said. “But the DSA doesn’t want the rest of the party in their tent. They want their own tent.

“He’s waving this big neon sign saying pay attention to this,” Del Percio added.

data.title: Divided we fall: Violent partisanship and the threat to national security
data.description:
Earlier this month, many paused to reflect upon the atrocities related to the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, wherein about 1,200 people were killed and more than 240 were taken hostage. One side calls Hamas a terrorist organization; the other accuses Israel of genocide for its response to this attack. Regardless of which side you are on, it cannot be denied that innocent men, women and children have been killed in both Israel and Gaza. 

Leaving the never-ending and increasingly acrimonious debate aside, I believe it is critically important to the national and economic security of the U.S. that we examine the months leading up to the attacks, giving us a window into an ever-evolving threat.   

Prior to Oct. 7, 2023, I reached out to a number of contacts in the political and military space with one basic question: “Do you fear that the increasing partisan, political protests taking place on the streets of Israel are serving as an all-consuming distraction which is causing the powers that be to take their eyes off the national security ball?”

As outlined by the London School of Economics and Political Science, “For nine months before the October 7 terrorist attack, Israelis took to the streets in their masses, with between 60,000 to 400,000 protesting weekly against the Netanyahu government’s judicial overhaul.” Though many of the massive protests were nonviolent, the police response was strong, involving stun grenades, water cannons and “a liquid known as ‘the skunk,’ a foul-smelling substance used by Israeli authorities for crowd control.”

Unfortunately, in the age of hyperpartisanship, hate and identity politics and social media, such destructive protests have become altogether too common, be they in Israel or the U.S.

I have long stressed that “human nature” should be inserted into every single equation. Human beings have biases and flaws, and can be indoctrinated and manipulated. Human bias is normal. But at a certain point, and in certain careers, be they in corporate America, the federal government, the military or academia, such bias must be controlled for the greater good of the nation.

Whether it’s here in America, deep in the “Age of Trump,” or in Israel, under the banner of Benjamin Netanyahu, emotions of adoration or hate were always seemingly on the razor’s edge. Either you totally agreed with leadership or you morphed into an “enemy” of the movement. But when does loyalty to a leader, an ideology or an identity become detrimental to the security of a nation and the safety of its people?

As but one example, when Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk was assassinated in 2025, there were literally thousands of posts from the “professional” class in the U.S. either rationalizing his murder or, worse, cheerleading it. These posts were from college professors, doctors, pilots, and administrators, just to name a few. But most alarming of all were the posts coming from members of the U.S. military celebrating the slaughter of a fellow human being for ideological reasons.

Sadly, though not surprisingly, polls such as from Harvard University found that 39 percent of young Americans believe political violence is acceptable under certain circumstances. Equally disturbing was a Politico-Public First survey that revealed more than one-third of Americans under age 45 believe political violence can be justified in certain cases.

Collectively, millions of young Americans may believe it’s now acceptable to kill a public figure because of political, ideological or identity politics differences. Rather than defeat them at the ballot box, or via the merits of a more convincing argument, some now apparently think executing a fellow American — a father, mother, brother or sister — is justified. How did our nation reach this level of depravity?

Our military and our three-letter-agencies have but one solemn duty: the protection of the U.S. and its people. Their allegiance cannot and must not be to one individual, one party, faith or identity. They cannot fall victim to bias, indoctrination, misinformation or unchecked egos.

As hate is amplified, as distractions grow and as protests turn violent, the truly patriotic young men and women in our military and our government must accomplish something almost superhuman: they must overcome their biases for the greater good of our nation and our people.

If they cannot, all will eventually be lost.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: Trump: California officials will 'go to jail' if state ignores DOJ voter roll suit
data.description:
President Trump reupped the Justice Department’s (DOJ) warning that California officials could face criminal charges if they include the mail-in ballots of the over 200,000 people the federal government identified as potential non-U.S. citizens in their midterm election count.

“They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Friday, sharing a copy of a letter the DOJ sent to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s Office.

The Justice Department sued California Thursday after providing state and local election officials with a USB drive containing voter roll citizenship data, giving the state 48 hours to compare 20,000 names the Department of Homeland Security flagged as non-U.S. citizens with its own data rolls.

The DOJ had sent a letter to these election officials earlier in the week, which included a handwritten password to access the files on the thumb drive. The department threatened legal action if they did not cross-reference the data. 

“If California was unable to independently confirm the citizenship of people on that list, the Federal Government asked that California set aside ballots received from them until the person’s citizenship was confirmed,” the lawsuit says.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) criticized the suit in a written response, calling it a “sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day.”

“The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials — who do a damn good job defending democracy — to violate federal law,” Newsom added.

A voting rights group sent a letter notifying the DOJ Wednesday they would seek a temporary restraining order if the administration didn’t abandon its plans.

“Your clients’ actions in compiling the list violates established law; your efforts to employ this list to systematically purge voters, less than a month before the election, further violates the National Voter Registration Act, among other laws,” attorneys for the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Voting Rights Project wrote in the letter.

In July, President Trump alleged California, along with three other states, collectively had 250,000 noncitizens on their voter rolls. Though a federal “preliminary review” of these lists, which DHS included in a letter sent to the states at the time, found less than half that number — 118,000 — matched the government had flagged.

The DOJ’s lawsuit comes less than 20 days before the November midterm elections.

data.title: Standing with farmers: Why US fertilizer independence matters
data.description:
This week, as we celebrate National Farmers Day and Global Fertilizer Day, we should remember a simple truth: Without farmers, there is no fertilizer industry, and without both farmers and the fertilizer industry, there is no reliable source of food. One-half of global food production can be attributed to the use of fertilizer.

Two American industries working together for a common good — even when times are tough.

It’s not an understatement to say that U.S. farmers are facing some of the most difficult economic times in recent history. The latest Department of Agriculture data tell a story farmers already know: Crop producers operated at negative profit margins throughout 2025 and continue to face similar headwinds in 2026. Interest rates, land rents and input costs remain elevated while commodity receipts have declined for three consecutive years.

The conflict in the Middle East has exposed critical vulnerabilities in the global supply chain and created additional volatility in the global fertilizer market. Damage to fertilizer production facilities and transportation challenges have limited exports from countries that rely on the Strait of Hormuz. 

Nearly 50 percent of global exports of sulfur, an important fertilizer, as well as a critical input to phosphate fertilizer production, move through this area. Likewise, between 30 and 50 percent of globally traded nitrogen fertilizer is now unavailable to reach its intended destinations, impacting farmers around the world, including those in the United States.

Regardless of the challenges, the fertilizer industry is deeply committed to supporting America’s farmers, as reflected in the investment decisions individual companies are making in domestic production and in broad support for expanded markets for farm commodities. Without profitable farmers, our industry cannot thrive.

Fertilizer is one of a farmer’s most critical tools to promote plant growth and improve crop yield and productivity, and to ensure farm profitability. When the reliable supply of fertilizers is threatened, the ripple effects are felt in every corner of rural America. For that reason, we believe that a resilient and growing U.S. fertilizer industry is vital to support the American farmer.

Just as U.S. farmers are among the most efficient and innovative in the world, so is the U.S. fertilizer sector. Individual fertilizer producers have publicly announced billions of dollars in new production facilities that help mitigate U.S. agriculture’s exposure to geopolitical disruptions. That’s why the Trump administration’s focus on boosting domestic fertilizer manufacturing is the right policy.

There are more than 100 fertilizer producers globally serving U.S. farmers, and the U.S. is one of only three nations with at least 20 unique companies producing fertilizer products. Still, fertilizer remains a global commodity with 90 percent of consumption occurring outside the United States. The issue is further complicated by the heavy involvement of state-owned entities on the international stage. Demand shocks in Asia or supply disruptions in the Middle East directly affect American farmers. 

This reality demands strategic resilience. When geopolitical events disrupt supply corridors, when export restrictions shift commodity flows, when currency swings alter product values overnight, American agriculture should not absorb the full shock of those disruptions. That is why both domestic fertilizer production capacity and global economic stability matter.

Policymakers must understand that fertilizer, food security and agricultural resilience are all interconnected and central to American prosperity. This is not a partisan issue. After all, Republicans and Democrats both depend on American agriculture to put food on their tables.

The path forward requires sound public policy. Farmers, retailers, policymakers and individual companies throughout the fertilizer supply chain each have essential roles. We can build a more resilient foundation by ensuring that policies encourage the expansion of markets for U.S. farm products and create conditions in which individual companies choose to invest in American fertilizer production. 

Corey Rosenbusch serves as The Fertilizer Institute’s president and CEO.

data.title: George Santos: 'I'd jump to serve' as White House press secretary
data.description:
Former Rep. George Santos (R-Fla.) pitched himself on Friday to fill the vacancy left by White House press secretary Katie Zacharia. 

“Hey I’m not technically open for a job because I have one already…. butttttttt… I’d jump to serve POTUS as press secretary in a heart beat. Just saying,” the former Republican lawmaker wrote on the social platform X.

A White House official announced Friday afternoon that Zacharia was “transitioning out” of her role after President Trump told reporters he advised the press secretary to “reconsider” her position. 

Zacharia’s five days on the job set a new record for the shortest-serving White House press secretary. 

She faced scrutiny over a shaky initial press conference, where she appeared visibly nervous, took only three reporter questions and presented herself as a lawyer on TV despite not passing the bar exam. 

Santos slammed Fox News host Sean Hannity after the anchor grilled Zacharia about her legal background during a Thursday interview. 

“F— you @seanhannity! You think you are untouchable and like to sit high on your horse and judged people,” he wrote on social media. 

The former lawmaker doubled down on his criticism of the Fox News host in a lengthy post on Friday evening, asking people who watched Hannity’s show to “unfollow” his X account.  

“I refuse to associate with people who think that the self-righteous pig known as Sean Hannity is the standard or barometer for anything in society,” Santos wrote. 

This is not the first time Santos has clashed with the Fox News host. Following his release from federal prison last fall, Hannity pressed the ex-congressman about whether he would repay the hundreds of thousands of dollars he stole to victims. Santos apologized but did not promise to pay back the amount. 

Santos was expelled from Congress in 2023 and convicted on multiple counts of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. President Trump commuted his sentence last October after the ex-congressman had served three months in prison. 

Since his departure from Congress, the Republican has continued to stir controversy. In August, he was issued a lifetime ban from the prediction market Kalshi after he failed to cooperate in an investigation into wagers he placed on the platform on this year’s State of the Union address.

data.title: Final Trump arch plans submitted to city omit proposed military complex
data.description:
Final site plans for President Trump’s proposed, 250-foot-tall triumphal arch do not mention the military features he previously said he would add to the project, according to documentation the Interior Department submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission.  

The president announced in late September the structure, slated to be built between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, would include a “top grade military complex” housing a large number of drones, snipers and ammunition. While such fortification was not part of the original proposal, Trump said it was added per the military’s “strong request.”

The latest project proposal, as shared with the planning commission, does not show any of the military features but does include other recent suggested changes — such as the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) recommended eternal flame. The D.C. planning agency is set to review the plans during its Nov. 5 meeting.

A White House official told The Washington Post on a condition of anonymity that Trump’s plans for the arch had not changed, rather, that the administration did not plan to publicly release any information about the project pertaining to national security at this stage.

The Post, who first reported on the final site plan, also cited an Interior Department spokesperson, Katie Martin, who said the current designs of the arch are capable of accommodating national security functions and more.

The Hill has reached out to the Interior Department for comment.

Trump’s plan to militarize the structure sparked concerns and criticism from lawmakers.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes Arlington, Va. — home to the National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport — criticized the plan to install a drone launching site directly in the landing path for incoming aircraft.

“Trump’s notion to make his vanity arch an ammunition depot for ‘snipers’ in a location where snipers have never been needed would place a large weapons cache within feet of thousands of tourists, pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers on major commuter traffic thoroughfares and Metro’s Blue Line,” Beyer said in a statement.

The FAA has concluded the arch would not pose a risk to airspace, according to a project evaluation published last month. Beyer argued the review did not take into account the presence of military drones.

Trump’s former national security adviser, John Bolton, called the idea to militarize the arch “not just wrong, it’s gonzo bonkers, it’s just completely divorced from reality.”

“That arch is going to be in the middle of a traffic circle. I don’t know what it’s defending against,” Bolton told MS NOW last month.

data.title: If the Supreme Court wants to protect freedom of the press, here is its chance
data.description:
This month, Journalist Catherine Herridge is in the fight of her life — and the stakes for the country could not be higher. The former Fox and CBS reporter has long been one of the most prominent investigative journalists in the U.S., particularly on national security stories. She is now on her last appeal to the Supreme Court, attempting to protect the most vital prerequisite of the free press: confidentiality of sources.

At issue is a 2017 story that aired on Fox News concerning a Virginia-based training firm patronized by Pentagon officials. Herridge exposed ties of the University of Management and Technology to the Chinese military. It was the kind of difficult, complex story that made Herridge such a respected figure in her profession. The subject of the story, University of Management and Technology founder Yanping Chen, sued, claiming that the exposure had led to her loss of employment.

Such lawsuits are usually brought against journalists by disgruntled subjects under defamation or other grounds that are quickly dismissed by courts. But Chen brought a novel claim against various officials under the Privacy Act. She alleges that they disclosed to Herridge protected information about an FBI investigation. Rather than sue Herridge directly, Chen subpoenaed her to disclose the names of her sources. Herridge sat for a deposition but refused to breach confidentiality.

This is not Herridge’s first rodeo in fighting for journalistic values. Years ago, CBS News forced her out and seized her files containing confidential source information. Despite considerable costs, Herridge eventually stared down the network and forced it to return the files.

Notably, much of the Fox News story about Chen was available in the public domain. For example, a whistleblower and FBI informant had said publicly that Chen had admitted to him that she had been a colonel in China’s People’s Liberation Army. He also alleged that she told him to lie about that fact when called to testify before a federal grand jury.

Because Herridge refuses to disclose her sources, we do not know how much she actually relied on non-public information. This puts her in an impossible position: She would have to reveal sources in order to show that Chen’s claims are meritless.

In making her Privacy Act claim, Chen cited the disclosure of many facts already available publicly, including contradictions of her denials on being part of the Chinese military. The only information that had not already appeared in the public domain appears to be photographic, including a picture of Chen in a Chinese colonel’s uniform.

In this case, Herridge had the misfortune of seeking relief in Washington, D.C., where judges have been relatively permissive in allowing such disputes to go to trial. In 2023, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, an Obama appointee, tossed aside protections that other circuit courts recognize under the First Amendment. He ordered Herridge to identify her confidential sources, then held her in contempt when she refused, imposing a crippling $800-a-day fine. Even that was not enough for Chen, who tried to have the penalties increased to $5,000 a day.

Before the fines were paused in August pending appeal, Herridge had to write a check every day from her two children’s college funds. “These fines are designed to break you emotionally and professionally,” she told me. “I would walk every day to the mailbox with our oldest son for emotional and moral support.”

Unfortunately, a panel of three judges on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Cooper’s ruling. Herridge therefore went to the Supreme Court for an emergency injunction against the daily fine. The court refused to intervene immediately, although Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated that he wanted to grant the relief.

Herridge is now back before the Supreme Court, which will have a final opportunity to take the case and prevent a catastrophic blow to press freedoms. If the court again punts, then any aggrieved subject of a news story could effectively strip journalistic sources of confidentiality by alleging a Privacy Act violation.

The cause of this pileup is the highly permissive standard adopted by the D.C. Circuit for the single most important jurisdiction for investigative reporting. To compel disclosure, Chen needs only to show that the source is central to her case and that she has exhausted other avenues of discovery. This test exposes every reporter who breaks a story in Washington involving government abuse or waste. Imagine if Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein had been sued under the Privacy Act by Nixon administration officials and forced to disclose the identity of Deep Throat.

Other circuits have a balancing test that allows for a more contextual resolution of such disputes. Another approach would be to deny such compelled disclosures when the case (as here) would not likely survive a motion for summary judgment. Chen, who lost her position because of information already in the public domain, cannot possibly show meaningful injuries from these photographs.

The irony in the case is crushing. Chen is an alleged former colonel in the People’s Liberation Army, using the U.S. Privacy Act to gut a Constitutional right not recognized in China. Of course she still has rights in this country, but the question is not whether she can sue under the Privacy Act — it is what standard she must meet before the courts make a journalist betray confidential sources.

Herridge got the story right and did the right thing in protecting her sources at great personal cost. The justices now have a chance to protect her. They should take her case. Not only has it created a split among the circuit courts, but it also has a compelling record to reconsider the confusing 1972 decision in Branzburg v. Hayes, which one appellate judge ridicules for being “about as clear as mud.”

Herridge is not seeking immunity or a favor. She is a tough reporter who just wants to do her job and protect her sources under a fair legal standard. The question is whether four justices will agree and grant review in Herridge v. Chen.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.” He previously worked for CBS News and currently works at Fox News as a legal analyst. His views do not necessarily reflect those of those networks.

data.title: Zelensky on Trump waiving Russia sanctions: 'This Act could have helped enormously'
data.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decried President Trump’s late-night decision to waive sanctions and tariffs against Russia days before they were set to take effect under a new law.

“At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” Zelensky wrote in Saturday morning statement posted to social platform X. 

“This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters,” the Ukrainian leader continued. 

The sweeping legislative sanctions package, which was named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), would have raised tariffs up to 100 percent on goods imported to the U.S. from the five largest purchasers of Russian fuel amid the country’s yearslong war against Ukraine. Trump signed the package into law last month.

On Friday night, the president issued an executive order that waived this sanction package, saying it was “in the national interests of the United States.” This followed his decision last week to ease sanctions on Russian oil, permitting the country to “immediately” begin selling 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets. 

These relief measures come amid rising fuel costs in the U.S. and abroad brought on by the Iran war, which have placed pressure on the Trump administration to address Americans’ affordability concerns ahead of the midterm elections. 

Ukraine and Russia have targeted each other’s energy infrastructure in recent military operations. Zelensky reported Saturday that Russia had “scaled up” these attacks, launching over 320 attack drones against Ukraine’s energy sector in a 12-hour period starting yesterday evening. 

The Ukrainian leader accused the Russian government of “trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine” before the winter season.

“Pressure is needed to stop this,” he said in his Saturday statement. “A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking.“

Zelensky added, “We must not give up ground. We must keep trying to end the war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely. I thank everyone who is truly fighting for peace and helping Ukraine!”

data.title: GOP lawmakers bash Trump's decision to waive Russia sanctions: 'Beyond irresponsible'
data.description:
Several GOP lawmakers criticized President Trump’s move to exempt Russia from the sanctions bill he signed law last month, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.) calling the move “Beyond irresponsible.”

Trump signed an executive order Friday evening to waive sanctions against Russia in a legislative package that was meant to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its military operations against Ukraine.

“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis wrote on the social platform X.

The legislation, signed by Trump in September, would impose tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

The sanctions bill was drafted by and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The late senator had announced a breakthrough on the legislation shortly before his death in July, saying lawmakers reached a deal with the White House to move it forward.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) posted the news on social media Saturday morning saying, “Lindsey would be appalled.”

“The President is prolonging the war, not ending it,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on social media, referring to Friday’s executive order.  

In his Friday order, the president noted that the legislation allows him to “waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person.”

“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”

One the other side of the aisle, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who played a major role in passing the sanctions bill, called the president’s move to waive sanctions for Russia, a “craven, cowardly action.”

“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal wrote in his post.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) also slammed the president’s move on social platform X, saying it “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.”

The move comes after the president struck a deal with Russia last week permitting the country to sell diesel products to the U.S. and in the world market amid global fuel shortages. The deal prompted backlash from lawmakers across the board.

In an interview with Piers Morgan, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” by the president’s decision.
